title: To the Edge of the Universe
subtitle: A zoom out through every scale, from the Sun to the cosmic horizon
intro: The observable universe spans ~93 billion light-years, yet on this logarithmic map it fits one view. This voyage pulls back one power of ten at a time — star, galaxy, supercluster, cosmic web, and finally the microwave glow of the Big Bang itself.

stops.label: The Sun
stops.narrative: Home. Every shell on this map is centred here — not because we are special, but because this is where we look from.

stops.label: The stars
stops.narrative: The nearest thousand light-years: the naked-eye stars, all inside one spiral arm of one galaxy.

stops.label: The Milky Way
stops.narrative: Pull back to 100,000 light-years and the whole galaxy — 100+ billion stars — is a single disc.

stops.label: The Local Group
stops.narrative: Andromeda, Triangulum and dozens of dwarfs — our galactic neighbourhood, a few million light-years across.

stops.label: The Local Supercluster
stops.narrative: The nearest galaxies from 2MRS trace the Virgo Cluster and the sheets threading the local universe.

stops.label: The cosmic web
stops.narrative: Billions of light-years out, SDSS galaxies trace filaments and voids — the largest structures that exist.

stops.label: The age of quasars
stops.narrative: Farther still we see only the brightest beacons: quasars, the blazing cores of young galaxies, their light billions of years old.

stops.label: The cosmic horizon
stops.narrative: The final shell is the cosmic microwave background at z≈1100 — the oldest light there is, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Beyond it lies the unobservable.
